name: Rainforest folk
one_line: The rain washes the soil out in a few seasons, so they farmed by moving: burn a patch, plant in the ash, walk away and let the forest close — and the forest itself is their ruin.

needs: a stream or river within 300 m (drink, fish, the canoe landing), and ground above its flood line for the garden and the posts

staples: manioc (bitter and sweet), taro and yam from the swidden
palm fruit (moriche, açaí) and brazil nut from the grove
how: swidden garden: burn, plant, three years, walk away
digging stick for tubers and cuttings
fish speared in the shallows, or a vine-poison pool
a wild hive smoked and cut; the grove gathered on the way past
preserve: manioc grated, squeezed and toasted to a flour that keeps for months
fish and game smoked on a rack over the hearth; honey in a gourd, nuts in the shell

fuel.note: wet wood barely burns: fronds and dead bamboo for the flame, wood dried on a rack over the hearth, candlenuts for light; the fire lives under the roof and is never let go out; only the dry forest has dead wood everywhere (branch, log, brush), and only half the year

shelter.form: the longhouse: one roof for several families on hardwood posts, palm thatch to the ground, a hearth and hammocks to each family; a raised floor where it floods; the house is rebuilt every generation and the site is not

TROPICAL_RAINFOREST.fuel: palm frond, dead bamboo along the river, wood dried over the fire
TROPICAL_RAINFOREST.food: manioc and taro in the swidden; brazil nut, moriche and açaí; river fish
TROPICAL_RAINFOREST.shelter: the longhouse: hardwood posts, palm thatch to the ground
TROPICAL_RAINFOREST.palette: black earth, wet green, thatch gold, annatto red

JUNGLE.fuel: bamboo above all; branch in the dry months
JUNGLE.food: hill rice and taro in the swidden, yam, banana; bamboo shoots
JUNGLE.shelter: bamboo walls and floor on stilts, grass or palm thatch
JUNGLE.palette: bamboo yellow-green, teak brown, monsoon grey

CLOUD_FOREST.fuel: bamboo thicket and branch, all of it damp; a drying rack over every hearth
CLOUD_FOREST.food: taro, highland banana and enset; the swidden closes slowly in the cold and the fallow is long
CLOUD_FOREST.shelter: a low house on the ground, bamboo and mud walls against the cold, the hearth inside, thatch to the eaves
CLOUD_FOREST.palette: moss green, mist white, grey bark, orchid pink

TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.fuel: branch and hardwood log: dead wood everywhere in the dry season; brush
TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.food: maize, beans and squash sown in the burn; manioc where it stays damp; fruit with the rains
TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.shelter: pole and thatch, wattle walls plastered with mud, a shade roof for the dry half of the year
TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.palette: dry gold, ash grey, peeling red bark, a green flush at the rains

knows: manioc: bitter from sweet, and the press
taro and giant taro (the corm cooked, never raw)
moriche and açaí palm fruit; brazil nut
annatto for paint and against insects
plantkeeper.teaches_flavour: why the nut grove stands where it does; why the black earth grows taller trees; why the swidden is left to close
plantkeeper.teaches_practical: bitter manioc kills raw: grate it, squeeze it in the woven press, toast the meal; the sweet kind boils; crush the poison vine in a still pool and the fish float up

makes: the sherds the black earth is made of

techniques.name: Swidden
techniques.verb: cut a garden-sized patch as the rains end, let it dry, burn it, plant manioc cuttings and taro in the ash; three years, then walk away and let the forest close; come back in thirty
techniques.teaches: the forest's crop and the restraint rule in one lesson: done small it is the most sustainable farming there is, done big it kills the forest — which is why the headman teaches this one first, before the grove
techniques.unlocks: the camp's crop ceiling; a swidden left to close comes back as forest, not scrub

techniques.name: Black earth
techniques.verb: hearth charcoal, bone and fish waste, broken pots, all raked into the garden and the midden for generations
techniques.teaches: a soil that keeps itself: the one thing these folk left that grows better than the land around it, two thousand years on
techniques.unlocks: a garden that never needs to move; the ruin's black earth

techniques.name: Forest garden
techniques.verb: plant the useful trees where you camp — nut, palm, fruit — and tend them on the way past
techniques.teaches: the forest remembers where people lived: a grove of the useful kind marks an old village long after the posts are gone
techniques.unlocks: groves cluster on old sites; the player can read a grove as a ruin

techniques.name: Digging stick
techniques.verb: a fire-hardened stick: dig tubers, plant cuttings
techniques.teaches: manioc grows from a stick of stem pushed into the ash and taro from the top of the last one: the crop that is its own seed
techniques.unlocks: the player plants and digs; a cutting in the store gets planted by a folk within days

techniques.name: Candlenuts
techniques.verb: string oil-rich nuts on a palm-leaf rib, light the top one; they burn down one after another
techniques.teaches: a short bright light where wet wood will not burn, and a clock: about a quarter of an hour a nut
techniques.unlocks: a hand light for the tropics; set in a split stick it is a lamp

techniques.name: Honey
techniques.verb: smoke the wild hive with a smouldering bundle, cut the comb out, leave the brood
techniques.teaches: the sweetest thing in the world, and the forest's gift to the exchange road

techniques.name: The burn
techniques.verb: in the dry forest, burn the fallow and the dry grass before the rains, a break cut round it first
techniques.teaches: here the burn is the swidden's season, not a separate craft; lit late in the dry it runs, and the camp walks

ladder: fire under the roof (wet wood: it is never let go out)
the swidden: manioc and taro in the ash — the crop
flour toasted dry, fish smoked, honey in gourds: storage
flour, pots and honey go downriver; salt and stone come up
growth.restraint: a garden-sized patch, never a field; three years and walk away, thirty to let the forest close; the black earth is how a village stays put — feed the soil instead of clearing more; the dry-forest burn only in season, the break cut first
growth.ceiling_hint: black earth on a river reaches the tribal ceiling (the ring villages and mound towns of the analogues); a poor-soil interfluve stays one longhouse; the cloud forest stays small, the swidden closes slowly in the cold

signatures.what: a patch of black soil under the litter where the rest of the forest is red or yellow; taller trees and more of the useful kind on it; charcoal and sherds all through it
signatures.restore: restored: the camp's garden goes on the black earth and never has to move
signatures.inherits: soil that stays rich: the crop ceiling without the fallow

signatures.what: brazil nut, peach palm, açaí and moriche in a stand where the wild forest would be a hundred kinds mixed: a village's orchard, planted and outliving the village
signatures.restore: cleared: the understory cut back and the grove reads as an orchard
signatures.inherits: fruit and nuts from the first season

signatures.what: an oval of low humps where the longhouse posts rotted, a hearth hollow in the middle, the ground blackest inside the ring
signatures.restore: restored: new posts in the old holes
signatures.inherits: a level dry floor on the deepest black earth

signatures.what: a cut in the bank trodden to a ramp, a dugout rotted to a trough in the mud
signatures.restore: cleared: the ramp re-cut, a new dugout beached on it
signatures.inherits: the fishing place and the river path

signatures.what: broken pots through the black earth, far more than a camp breaks by accident: the potter's waste, worked in on purpose; red and white paint gone to pink
signatures.restore: restored: the potter finds the old clay pit and the new sherds go into the same ground
signatures.inherits: the clay pit is dug: the potter comes sooner

ruin.plants_differ: a grove of the useful kind (nut, palm, fruit) where the wild forest is mixed; taller, faster growth on the black earth; papaya, chili and cotton gone wild at the old clearing's edge

aesthetic.silhouette: one long roof to the ground in a clearing of burnt stumps, smoke leaking through the thatch; tall nut trees standing over it
sounds: the rasp of the grater, the press dripping
props: the manioc press hanging from a post
a rack of fuel drying over the hearth

huts.workshop_form: a low open-sided shed of hardwood posts and palm thatch to the ground on the river side, bamboo rails and a raised slat floor, bark-and-liana lashing at every joint, smoke leaking from the longhouse beside it
soft: a woven manioc press hung from a post, a stick through its loop
liana and bark fibre soaking in a trough, a hank being twisted into cord
a fish trap of split bamboo half woven
palm leaf strips laid out for a mat
hard: a dugout paddle blank on a log, shell-scraped
a fire-hardened digging stick, its point turned in the coals
bamboo split into strips with a wedge, a row of knives of it
a bone awl and fish-bone needles in a gourd
hearth: the manioc griddle on three stones, meal toasting
a smoke rack of river fish over a green-wood fire
a rack of fuel drying over the embers
candlenuts strung on a palm rib, the top one lit
kiln: a clay hump kiln stacked with bamboo and bark, downwind
pots and urns drying in the shade, annatto-red slip on the rims
the clay pit by the stream, a heap of burnt bark temper beside it
huts.porch_sign: a woven manioc press hanging from the porch post, dripping
huts.library: a small thatched hut raised on posts above the flood line, beside the longhouse; the winter-count is painted on a sheet of beaten bark in annatto red and soot
third_places: the dugout on the landing in the rain

real_world.analogue: Kuikuro and the upper Xingu peoples
real_world.region: upper Xingu, Mato Grosso, Brazil — living peoples on village sites hundreds to thousands of years old
real_world.note: still make dark earth (eegepe) on purpose: middens of food waste and ash near the village centre, ash and charcoal spread on fields and round the base of trees; the ancient dark earth under their sites is enriched in the same carbon and phosphorus. Across Amazonia such earth was made c. 450 BCE–950 CE from charcoal, bone, broken pottery and compost, lies up to 2 m deep, holds seventy times the carbon of the soil around it and is still fertile. Bitter manioc is the staple, grated, squeezed and toasted

real_world.region: Marajó island, mouth of the Amazon, c. 800–1400 CE
real_world.note: earth mounds (tesos) filled with refuse to stand above the flood, malocas in concentric ovals, polychrome funerary urns; açaí and fish taken with poison lianas; perhaps 100,000 people

shifting cultivation: sweet potato four to five years, yam and taro five to six, manioc four to six; some 250 food plants and 650 medicinal; forest islands (apêtê) planted in the savanna and shielded with cool fires — how many were made from nothing is debated; women manage most of the fire

real_world.region: Wahgi valley, Papua New Guinea highlands
real_world.note: taro planted about 9,000 years ago in drained swamp, banana and sugarcane by 6,900–6,400 years ago; wooden digging sticks found; UNESCO 2008 — a crop in the highlands, one of the places farming began on its own
the dry-forest swidden: two years of maize, beans and squash (and a dozen more), eight years fallow; called one of the most successful human inventions ever

real_world.region: Ituri forest, Congo basin — living people
real_world.note: forest foragers: wild honey in season, net hunting, leaf-and-sapling huts lashed with vine; meat and forest goods exchanged with farming villagers for pots, iron and crops
